defaults.teacher_persona: A SOC analyst who treats every alert as a question about evidence and says out loud when a signal is not yet enough to act on.
classmates: A support technician who forwards alerts to the SOC and wants to know what happens next
An administrator who owns the accounts and is wary of breaking access while tightening it
defaults.interaction: Case-led: the teacher hands over a real-looking signal, the classmates state what they would do and what it would cost, and the group decides what evidence would justify escalating.
defaults.assessment: Each classroom ends with 3-5 checks aligned to the chapter's graded activity.

classrooms.title: What the SOC Sees, and What You Feed It
classrooms.prompt: Explain what a security operations centre collects and decides, and where a support technician sits in that loop. Give the classmates a set of alerts and tickets and have them triage: which are noise, which need enrichment, and which should wake someone up.
objectives: Describe the SOC's collect, detect, and respond loop
Triage an alert by impact and confidence rather than by novelty
Hand an alert over with the evidence attached

activities.title: Which of these five alerts is real?

classrooms.title: Identity Is the Control Plane
classrooms.prompt: Work through least privilege, account lifecycle, and privileged access, then run an access review: the classmates get a list of accounts and group memberships and must justify each one, revoke what is not needed, and say what breaks when they do.
objectives: Apply least privilege to a real set of accounts and groups
Run a joiner/mover/leaver check and spot the orphaned account
Explain what an access change costs before making it

activities.title: Least privilege and the account lifecycle

classrooms.title: Layers, So One Failure Is Not Enough
classrooms.prompt: Teach defense in depth through the controls a support technician actually touches: EDR and antivirus, host firewalls, patching, network segmentation, and email filtering. Then have the classmates harden a machine step by step and argue about which single control failing would hurt most.
objectives: Name the endpoint and network controls that make up a layered defense
Harden a workstation without breaking the user's work
Explain why one failed control should not be a breach

activities.title: Malware on a laptop: the first ten minutes

classrooms.title: Rehearsed, Not Improvised
classrooms.prompt: Walk the incident-response lifecycle from prepare to lessons learned, then run a tabletop: a confirmed account compromise on a Friday afternoon. The classmates must confirm the incident, contain it without destroying evidence, communicate upward, and write the timeline they would hand to a review.
objectives: Follow the incident lifecycle in order and know what each phase produces
Contain an incident while preserving the evidence
Write a timeline and lessons-learned note that survives review

activities.title: Prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover, learn
A compromised account on Friday afternoon
Debrief: what the timeline must show
